sections.h2: Where to record a Pima County deed
sections.html:
Land in Pima County is recorded at the Pima County Recorder's Office in Tucson, since state law makes the county of the property the place to file. Under A.R.S. 33-411, a later buyer or lender who paid value and had no notice isn't bound by an instrument that was never recorded in that county. Signing a deed doesn't finish the job; getting it onto the public record does.

Online, the Recorder offers record searches, e-recording, document pickup and a document services subscription. Maps to its two Tucson sites, 240 N Stone Avenue and 6920 E Broadway Boulevard, sit on the home page. Confirm current hours on the contact page before you go.

The office also runs elections and voter registration, so much of the site is about voting. For deed help, look for the Recording Fees, Recording Requirements and Recording FAQ links.

The usual charge is $30 for each instrument, set by A.R.S. 11-475 for papers the law requires or permits to be recorded. A government party that requests the recording pays $15. Section 11-475.01's amount is already inside the $30.

Price plays no part, since the county schedule lists only per-document charges. If you suspect another charge applies to your deed, check with the title company or the state Department of Revenue.

ChargeAmount
Recording any document$30.00
Government agency recording$15.00
Return of improperly submitted document$5.00 per document
Returned check$25.00
Certified copy$1.00 per image, plus $3.00 per certificate
Mail processing$1.00 per document

The office takes Visa, Mastercard, cash, checks and money orders, made payable to Pima County Recorder. Card payment is limited to the counter; phone and mail orders can't use one. Buying online adds a 2 percent card convenience fee.

Two rules sink many mailed packets.

  • Your name has to be pre-printed on the check.
  • Any check or money order must carry a date within 60 days of receipt.

No charge applies to military discharge papers under A.R.S. 11-465. A copy of a recorded document costs $0.25 per standard letter-size image, or $0.25 per digital document. Plats and survey maps are priced apart, at $24 for image one and $20 for each image after it.

sections.h2: What a deed must look like
sections.html:
Expect to supply a caption, original signatures, a legible original or copy and a legal description, along with an affidavit of property value unless the transfer is exempt. The layout rules sit on the Recording Requirements page and in A.R.S. 11-480; fall short and the counter may reject the document.

  • Title the instrument with a short caption, for example warranty deed.
  • Keep pages within 8 1/2 by 14 inches and type at ten point or larger.
  • Leave half-inch margins, and reserve the top two inches of page one for the recording stamp.
  • If you are modifying an earlier document, cite its recording date and its docket and page or sequence number.

The grantor has to sign the deed and acknowledge it before an authorized officer (A.R.S. 33-401). The County Attorney's Office has told Recorder staff not to give legal advice, so ask an attorney or title company which deed fits.

sections.h2: Why a Pima County deed comes back
sections.html:
Most returns trace to a short list of causes: no caption, margins that crowd the stamp area, a missing signature or acknowledgment, no affidavit or exemption notation, or a check that is undated, unprinted with your name or older than 60 days. A returned document costs $5, and a bounced check costs $25, on top of the delay.

Mailing adds $1 per document for processing, so a mailed deed with a check for $30 should include that extra dollar. Compare your packet with the list above before you seal the envelope, and ask your title company to look over the deed if the sale is on a tight schedule, because a rejected deed can push your closing date.

Walk-in customers recording a document show valid photo ID, as A.R.S. 11-472 requires. Acceptable choices are a state driver's license or ID card, a tribal enrollment card or other tribal ID, or any ID issued by a federal, state or local government.

The rule excludes documents brought by an escrow officer, a title insurer or agent, a chartered bank or credit union, a practicing member of the State Bar of Arizona, or a governmental entity. Most sellers never see it, because escrow files the deed. A recorder may jot down the ID's type, name and number but may not copy it, and that note isn't public.

sections.h2: Affidavit of property value and exemptions
sections.html:
Both buyer and seller sign this form, and it travels with the deed to the counter. Without a complete one, or an exemption notation, the Recorder must refuse the deed (A.R.S. 11-1133). The questions cover both names, the legal description, the sale date, the total consideration and owner-occupied versus rental use. Get the form from the Arizona Department of Revenue.

Certain transfers are excused by A.R.S. 11-1134, including these:

  • Gifts by deed.
  • Quitclaim deeds with no money exchanged.
  • Trustee's deeds after a deed of trust, and transfers made only to give or release security for a debt.
  • Homes passed for token consideration among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings.
  • Beneficiary-deed transfers for token consideration.

If you claim an exemption, the Department of Revenue exemption letter and number must accompany the deed at recording. Your title company can verify the exact notation first.

sections.h2: Pima County housing context and next steps
sections.html:
Pima County is home to an estimated 1,074,685 people, with Tucson as seat and largest city. Housing units are 65.2 percent owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied home is worth $319,700. Recording is identical across the county. Taxes are billed separately by the Pima County Treasurer at 240 N. Stone Avenue, which can quote an amount before closing.

Here is a workable order: check the deed's caption and margins, sign before a notary, finish the affidavit or note the exemption, then have the escrow or title office record it. Delivering it yourself? Bring photo ID and a $30 check payable to Pima County Recorder, dated within 60 days. Cash sales follow the same steps, minus a buyer's lender, so usually no loan document is recorded behind your deed.

faqs.q: What does Pima County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: $30 for each document, or $15 if a government agency requests it. Getting a document back for being improperly submitted costs $5, and a returned check costs $25.

faqs.q: Does Pima County tax the sale of a home when the deed is recorded?
faqs.a: Nothing on the Recorder's schedule depends on price. You pay the flat fee and file an affidavit of property value. Ask your title company or the Department of Revenue about any other charge.

faqs.q: Will Pima County Recorder staff help me complete a deed?
faqs.a: No, the County Attorney's Office has told them not to give legal advice. Use an attorney, escrow officer or title company to prepare it, and the Recorder reviews it against the form rules.

faqs.q: Is photo ID required to record in person in Pima County?
faqs.a: Yes, with exceptions for exempt submitters such as escrow offices, title insurers, banks, credit unions, State Bar members and government entities. The rule is A.R.S. 11-472.

faqs.q: What happens if a Pima County deed is never recorded?
faqs.a: A later buyer or lender who paid value without notice isn't bound by it (A.R.S. 33-411). The new owner is exposed, so record soon after closing.
